questions.q:
Assertion (A): Specific rituals and festivals, such as Vasanta Panchami and Sharad Purnima, are associated with the ritus.
Reason (R): Depending on the region, some trees shed their leaves or change colour as sharad approaches.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The tree behaviour is a separate sign of the season; it does not explain why festivals are tied to the ritus.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Asha tells her cousin, 'Seasons repeat every year because the weather of a place keeps changing from day to day.' Their teacher says the explanation is wrong. Which explanation does the chapter give for seasons?
questions.a: Seasons occur as the Earth revolves around the Sun, last a few months and recur every year. Weather changes inside a season; climate is the long-term pattern and does not change with each season.
o: Seasons occur as the Earth revolves around the Sun, last a few months each and recur every year.
Seasons occur when the climate of a region changes, each lasting a few months before a new climate begins.
Seasons occur because winds reverse their direction every few months, which only monsoon regions experience.
Seasons occur when the weather of a region changes, each lasting a few days and then recurring every month.

questions.q: The monthly rainfall (mm, January to December) of a coastal town is: 5, 5, 10, 10, 35, 180, 290, 270, 160, 20, 10, 5. Which statement does this table support, using the chapter's idea of seasons?
questions.a: June to September carry 180 + 290 + 270 + 160 = 900 mm of the 1,000 mm year (90 percent): a specific rainy period, which the chapter says India has along with the four usual seasons.
o: Rain is concentrated in one four-month spell, which fits a rainy season in addition to the usual four.
Rain falls in all twelve months, so the town has no season of its own and only its weather changes.
Rain is heaviest in June, so the town has a climate of its own and the other months are all weather.
Rain is spread evenly over the year, so the town has four main seasons and no separate rainy season.

questions.q: The six ritus come in the order vasanta, grishma, varsha, sharad, hemanta, shishir, and the cycle then begins again. (a) Counting forward from vasanta, how many steps lead to sharad? (b) Counting on from sharad, how many more steps bring the cycle back to vasanta?
questions.a: (a) 3 steps (grishma, varsha, sharad). (b) 3 more steps (hemanta, shishir, vasanta). Together 6 steps, a full cycle that recurs every year.
s: Part (a): 3 steps
Part (b): 3 more steps, 6 in all

questions.q: Ravi argues: 'Climate is a long-term pattern, so once a region has a climate it can never change.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the climate remains stable over long periods, yet changes have been recorded in recent decades and many are caused by human actions.
o: Climate is usually stable, but changes have been recorded in recent decades, many caused by human actions.
Climate stays fixed for ever; the changes recorded in recent decades are only weather and have human causes.
Climate changes every season, so scientists record a new climate each year and human actions play no part.
Climate changes only through natural processes, so the recorded changes of recent decades have no human cause.

questions.q:
The Eco Club of a school in a small Rajasthan town has kept the highest noon temperature of every June for the last 12 years (degrees C): 41, 42, 40, 43, 44, 41, 42, 43, 45, 42, 44, 43. Two lines are drafted for the notice board. Line 1: 'On 14 June this year the noon temperature touched 45.' Line 2: 'June noons in our town are 40 C or more.' The principal wants Line 2 printed in the school prospectus as the town's climate.
(a) Which line is weather and which is climate-type information? Find the mean of the 12 readings.
(b) The chapter says a climate is described over three decades or more. What fraction of that period does the club's record cover?
(c) A member says, 'Because all 12 readings are 40 or above, the climate of the town is proved hot.' Evaluate this.
(d) Should the club print Line 2 as 'climate' now, or print it as a 12-year record and keep recording? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Line 1 is weather (one day); Line 2 is a pattern, climate-type information. Mean = 510 / 12 = 42.5 C. (b) 12 / 30 = 2/5 (40 percent) of the minimum period. (c) Not proved: a consistent pattern is a good sign, but 12 years is short of three decades, so it is a strong hint, not a description of climate. (d) Credit either choice with reasons from the data and chapter: printing it as a 12-year record keeps the prospectus accurate while the club continues to 30 years; printing it as climate now is acceptable only if the line states that it rests on 12 years of records. A bare claim of climate with no limit stated fails.
s: Part (a): Line 1 weather, Line 2 pattern; mean 42.5 C
Part (b): 12/30 = 40 percent
Part (c): pattern suggestive but 12 years is short of three decades
Part (d): a decision tied to three decades with the limit stated

questions.q:
Match each remark in Column A with the idea it illustrates in Column B.
Column A: 1. 'A dusty wind blew over Jaipur this afternoon.'  2. 'Jaipur has had dry summers year after year.'  3. 'The trees on our street are shedding leaves.'  4. 'Besides the four usual seasons, our country has a separate period of heavy rain every year.'
Column B: a. climate  b. weather  c. plant life in rhythm with a ritu  d. the rainy season (monsoon) in addition to four usual seasons

Two pupils from different states write that, as the cold season nears, trees near their homes behave differently: in Tara's town the trees are shedding leaves, while in Uday's town the trees are changing colour. A third pupil says one of them must be mistaken. What does the chapter allow?
questions.a: The chapter says that depending on the region some trees shed their leaves or change their colour as sharad (autumn) approaches, so both observations fit.
o: Both can be right, since depending on the region trees shed leaves or change colour as autumn nears.
Tara alone is right, since the chapter says every tree in India sheds its leaves when autumn approaches.
Uday alone is right, since the chapter says colour change is the only sign that autumn approaches.
Neither is right, since trees respond to the weather of a single day and not to the season.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. A place can have very different weather in two seasons without any change in its climate.
2. Seasons recur every year because the weather of the place keeps changing.
3. Most regions have four main seasons, yet India has the rainy season (monsoon) as well in the same year.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
questions.a: 1 and 3 are correct. 2 is false: seasons recur because the Earth revolves around the Sun, not because the weather changes.

questions.q: The chapter says seasons are related 'to both' weather and climate. Give one example showing the link to weather and one showing the link to climate.
questions.a: Weather: the weather changes with the season, e.g. dry and hot in summer months, humid and rainy in the monsoon. Climate: the pattern of seasons in a region is closely connected with the climate, e.g. India has a rainy season along with the other four.
s: An example of weather changing with a season
An example of the pattern of seasons reflecting climate

questions.q: A village shop owner sees that woollen sales, cold-drink sales and umbrella sales each peak in a different spell of the year, spell after spell, year after year. He says, 'Sales follow the weather of the week.' A customer disagrees. Which reply fits the chapter best?
questions.a: Human life is in rhythm with the ritus: the food we eat and the clothes we wear change with the season, and seasons recur every year.
o: Sales follow the ritus: the clothes and food people choose change with the season, which recurs every year.
Sales follow the climate alone: the clothes people choose change only when the decades-long pattern shifts.
Sales follow the weather alone: the clothes people choose change each day, so the spells have no yearly cycle.
Sales follow the festivals alone: the food and clothes people choose depend on rituals and not on any season.

questions.q: True or False: 'Climate is the weather of the coming week, because both describe what the air is doing.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Weather is what we experience hour to hour or day to day and keeps changing; climate is the pattern of weather over a long period, several decades at least, so a week cannot be the climate.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: climate is the long-term pattern over several decades at least, weather is day-to-day

questions.q: Why does the chapter say that the weather of a place is different in every season, yet the pattern of seasons points to its climate?
questions.a: In each season the weather differs: dry and hot in summer months, humid and rainy in the monsoon. Yet the same cycle of seasons repeats in the region year after year, and that long-term pattern is its climate.
s: Weather varies with the season, with an example
The repeating pattern of seasons is connected with the climate

questions.q: Mira's grandmother says the year has six ritus, her teacher says it has five seasons, and her atlas says most regions have four. (a) Explain how all three counts can be correct. (b) Which count suits India's rainfall pattern in the chapter's account, and why?
questions.a: (a) Most regions have four main seasons; India has the rainy season (monsoon) along with those four, making five; traditionally many parts of India divide the year into six ritus. (b) Five seasons (or six ritus) because India gets rainfall in a specific period, which a four-season count would not show.
s: Part (a): four main seasons in most regions, a fifth rainy season in India, six traditional ritus
Part (b): the count that includes the rainy season, with the reason

questions.q: Imran says, 'It was 41 degrees C in Nagpur on 3 May, so Nagpur has a hot climate.' Is his reasoning sound? Explain.
questions.a: His conclusion may turn out to be true, but one day's reading is weather and cannot prove climate. Climate is the pattern of weather over several decades at least, so he needs many years of records, not a single temperature.
s: Verdict: the reasoning is not sound
Reason: one day's temperature is weather
What is needed: the pattern over several decades at least

questions.q:
The weather log of a house in Pune reads: Monday heavy rain 24 C; Tuesday drizzle 25 C; Wednesday cloudy 27 C; Thursday bright sun 31 C; Friday heavy rain 23 C. Records kept by the same family for 40 years show that Pune's June to September months have been wet every year.
(i) Separate the information into weather and climate, with a reason.
(ii) Name the season the log belongs to and say what makes such a season recur.
(iii) Explain how the log's changing days can sit alongside a stable climate.
questions.a: (i) The five daily entries are weather (what is experienced day to day, keeps changing); 'wet June to September for 40 years' is climate (a pattern over several decades at least). (ii) The rainy season or monsoon; seasons recur every year as the Earth revolves around the Sun. (iii) Weather varies by the day (24, 25, 27, 31, 23 C), but across many years the same wet pattern repeats in these months, and that long-term pattern is the climate.
s: Weather entries identified with reason
Climate statement identified with reason (decades)
Rainy season/monsoon named
Recurrence through the Earth revolving around the Sun
Daily changes sit inside a long-term pattern

questions.q: A cultural club plans three events and fixes dates by the weather forecast of the week: a vasanta festival, a sharad festival and a rainy-season fair. A teacher says the dates should be fixed by the ritus, not by the week's weather. Give two reasons from the chapter in support of the teacher.
questions.a: Seasons recur every year as the Earth revolves around the Sun, so a ritu can be relied on year after year, whereas weather keeps changing from day to day. Specific rituals and festivals are associated with the ritus (e.g. Vasanta Panchami, Sharad Purnima). Also, plant and animal life are in rhythm with the ritus, so the festival signs (blooms, leaf fall) follow the ritu, not a week's weather.
s: Seasons recur each year, weather keeps changing
Rituals and festivals are associated with the ritus, with an example
Life is in rhythm with the ritus (a sign tied to the ritu)

questions.q:
A school culture club makes a wall calendar of its village's year. It has eight entries: Vasanta Panchami (1 entry), a fair after the first heavy rains of the year (2 entries linked to the rainy season), Sharad Purnima and leaf-fall (2 entries), pre-winter evening bonfires (1 entry) and woollens and thick-furred goats in the coldest weeks (2 entries). Nothing has been placed for the hot dry months before the rains.
(a) Place each group of entries in one of the six traditional ritus and say which ritu is empty.
(b) If the calendar has only four columns (spring, summer, autumn, winter), which entries have no column of their own?
(c) Compare a six-column plan with a five-column plan (spring, summer, rainy season, autumn, winter) by writing how many entries fall in each column of each plan, treating pre-winter and winter entries as one column in the five-column plan.
(d) The club has room for only one plan. Which would you recommend, and why?
questions.a: (a) Vasanta Panchami: vasanta (1); fair after the first rains: varsha (2); Sharad Purnima and leaf-fall: sharad (2); bonfires: hemanta (1); woollens and thick fur: shishir (2); the empty ritu is grishma (summer). (b) The two rainy-season entries, since the chapter says India has a rainy season along with the other four seasons, which the four columns leave out. (c) Six columns: vasanta 1, grishma 0, varsha 2, sharad 2, hemanta 1, shishir 2. Five columns: spring 1, summer 0, rainy season 2, autumn 2, winter 3 (hemanta and shishir merged). (d) Credit a reasoned choice: six columns keep pre-winter (1 entry) apart from the coldest weeks and match the traditional ritus tied to festivals; five columns are simpler and still show the monsoon but merge the pre-winter and winter entries (3 in all) into one column. A choice with no reference to the counts fails.
s: Part (a): groups placed correctly; grishma empty
Part (b): the two rainy-season entries have no column
Part (c): counts for both plans correct
Part (d): a choice supported by the counts and the ritus

questions.q: Write a short diary entry of three lines for a village child in which a plant, an animal and a human activity each show the child that a particular ritu has begun, without naming the ritu. Then name the ritu you meant and the chapter statement that supports each clue.
questions.a: Any valid entry, e.g. 'The trees by the road are shedding leaves; the village is preparing for Sharad Purnima; we are changing our clothes for the cooler days.' Ritu: sharad (autumn). Support: the chapter says that as sharad approaches some trees shed leaves or change colour, festivals such as Sharad Purnima are associated with it, and the clothes we wear change with the season. (Credit consistent alternatives, e.g. thick fur of animals in the cold winter months.)
s: Entry with a plant, an animal and a human clue (or three clues that fit one ritu)
The ritu named correctly and consistently with the clues
Each clue tied to a chapter statement

questions.q: A school notice says: 'Our festivals follow nature, not the clock.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Include (i) what the chapter says about the six ritus and festivals, (ii) two other ways in which life is in rhythm with the ritus, and (iii) one reason why such rhythms differ from region to region.
questions.a: (i) The year is divided traditionally into six ritus: vasanta, grishma, varsha, sharad, hemanta, shishir; specific rituals and festivals such as Vasanta Panchami and Sharad Purnima are associated with them. (ii) Crops grown, food eaten and clothes worn change with the season; animals develop thick fur in the cold winter months. (iii) Depending on the region, some trees bloom in vasanta while elsewhere they shed leaves or change colour as sharad approaches, so the signs differ by region.
s: The six ritus named with their link to festivals
Two ways of life in rhythm with ritus
Regional difference with an example

questions.q:
A state cooperative has Rs 40 lakh and must spend all of it on one project. Project 1: a water-collection scheme costing Rs 1.6 lakh per village, for villages of region S, which has extremely hot days, cool nights and very little rainfall. Project 2: one rice-and-spice processing unit costing Rs 40 lakh, to be set up in region R, which has heavy rainfall in the monsoon months. Regions P (very hot summers, cold winters) and Q (hot summers, mild winters, moderate rainfall in the rainy season) are not covered by either project.
(a) Name the climate type of each of S and Q.
(b) How many villages can Project 1 cover?
(c) A councillor suggests putting the processing unit in P because it is easier to reach. Using the chapter, say what P is known for and why that does not suit a rice-and-spice unit.
(d) Which project would you fund? Justify with the climate information.
questions.a: (a) S is arid; Q is semi-arid. (b) 40 / 1.6 = 25 villages. (c) P is the subtropical northern plains, where most of India's wheat is grown; rice and spices are linked with the heavy rainfall of the western coastal strip (R), so raw material would have to be brought from far. (d) Either choice with climate-based reasons: Project 1 helps 25 villages where very little rainfall makes saving water essential; Project 2 ties a large sum to one site where heavy monsoon rain favours rice and spices. Credit a decision that weighs the 25 villages against one unit and names the climate on which it relies.
s: Part (a): S arid, Q semi-arid
Part (b): 25 villages
Part (c): P is wheat country; rice and spices go with R, the tropical wet coast
Part (d): a funded choice justified with the climate

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Thar receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon months.
Reason (R): People in the Thar have had to develop unique ways to collect and save water.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
questions.a: The Assertion is false: the Thar has an arid climate with very little rainfall; heavy monsoon rainfall belongs to the western coastal strip. The Reason is true, and it points to scarcity, which contradicts the Assertion.

questions.q: A district has hot summers, mild winters and only moderate rainfall, which falls in the rainy season. It is drier than the western coastal strip but wetter than the Thar, so the chapter's climate type for it is ___.
questions.a: semi-arid

questions.q: A tourist leaflet says, 'Hill stations enjoy the same cold, snowy winters as the highest Himalayan villages.' Which correction agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Hill stations lie in the temperate climate of the lower Himalayas and hilly areas: moderately cold winters and summers not too hot. Cold, snowy winters belong to the alpine climate of the high Himalayas.
o: Hill stations are temperate, with moderately cold winters; snowy winters belong to the alpine Himalayas.
Hill stations have a subtropical climate with very hot summers; snowy winters belong to the northern plains.
Hill stations have a tropical wet climate with heavy monsoon rain; snowy winters belong to the western coast.
Hill stations have a semi-arid climate with mild winters; snowy winters belong to the Deccan Plateau.

questions.q: Compare three climates in the chapter: subtropical (northern plains), semi-arid (central Deccan Plateau) and tropical (eastern India and the southern peninsula). Which feature do the second and the third share that the first does not?
questions.a: Semi-arid has mild winters and tropical has a mild winter, while the subtropical plains have cold winters. Distinct wet and dry periods belong to the tropical climate alone; heavy monsoon rainfall belongs to the west coast.
o: A mild winter in the cool months
Cold winters after very hot summers
Heavy rainfall in the monsoon months
Distinct wet and dry periods in the year

questions.q: Water engineers rank three regions by their need to save water, using only the rainfall the chapter gives: the Thar, the central Deccan Plateau and the western coastal strip. (a) Rank them from greatest to least need. (b) Support the order with the rainfall wording the chapter uses for each.
questions.a: (a) Thar, then the Deccan Plateau, then the western coastal strip. (b) Thar: very little rainfall; Deccan: moderate rainfall during the rainy season; western coast: heavy rainfall during the monsoon months.
s: Part (a): Thar > Deccan > west coast
Part (b): very little / moderate in the rainy season / heavy in monsoon months

questions.q: In May, Pranav leaves a hill station, where summers are not too hot and winters are moderately cold, and travels down to the northern plains. Comparing the chapter's two climate types, what change should he expect?
questions.a: Hill stations (temperate): summers not too hot, winters moderately cold. Northern plains (subtropical): very hot summers and cold winters, so hotter summers and colder winters.
o: Hotter summers and colder winters
Hotter summers and milder winters
Cooler summers and colder winters
Cooler summers and milder winters

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The whole Himalayan range has a temperate climate.
2. Eastern India and the southern peninsula have a mild winter and distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds.
3. People from the plains go to hill stations for relief from the heat because their summers are not too hot.
Which statements are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: 2 and 3 are correct. 1 is false: only the lower Himalayas and many hilly areas are temperate; the high Himalayas have an alpine climate.

questions.q: A relief agency can pre-position water tankers in only one of these regions before the dry summer. Judging only by the rainfall each region's climate description gives, where is the need to save water greatest?
questions.a: The chapter gives the Thar very little rainfall, the Deccan moderate rainfall in the rainy season, and the western coast heavy monsoon rainfall; the plains' description speaks of temperature, not scarce rain. People in the Thar had to develop unique ways to collect and save water.
o: The Thar, where the climate is arid with very little rainfall
The Deccan Plateau, where rain is moderate and comes in the rainy season
The western coastal strip, where rain is heavy in the monsoon months
The northern plains, where summers are very hot and winters are cold

questions.q: Nisha says, 'Eastern India and the southern peninsula have the same climate as the western coastal strip, because both are called tropical.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter calls the western coastal strip tropical wet (heavy monsoon rainfall, rice and spices) and the east and south tropical (mild winter, distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds).
o: The west coast is tropical wet with heavy rain; the east and south have a mild winter and wet and dry spells.
Both are tropical wet, since both receive heavy rainfall in the monsoon months and favour rice and spices.
The east and south are tropical wet; the west coast is semi-arid, with moderate rainfall in the rainy season.
The west coast is tropical with a mild winter; the east and south are tropical wet with heavy monsoon rain.

questions.q: A student writes: 'Eastern India and the southern peninsula are dry all year and have a harsh winter.' Correct the two errors using the chapter and name the climate type.
questions.a: The climate is tropical. It has a mild winter, not a harsh one, and distinct wet and dry periods controlled by the monsoon winds, so it is not dry all year.
s: Winter is mild, not harsh
Distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds; the climate is tropical

questions.q: Zoya says, 'The Himalayas and the hill stations have the same climate because both are hilly.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The high Himalayas have an alpine climate with cold, snowy winters and cool summers. Lower in the Himalayas and in many hilly areas the climate is temperate, with moderately cold winters and summers not too hot, which is where hill stations lie. Being hilly does not give the same climate.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Himalayas: alpine, cold snowy winters, cool summers
Hill stations: temperate, moderately cold winters, summers not too hot

questions.q: (a) A reporter writes, 'Being a desert, the Thar is scorching at every hour.' Correct this using the chapter's description. (b) The reporter adds that the northern plains share the Thar's climate because both have very hot summers. Name two features that separate the two climates.
questions.a: (a) The Thar has extremely hot days but cool nights. (b) The Thar is arid with very little rainfall, while the northern plains are subtropical with cold winters and most of India's wheat.
s: Part (a): extremely hot days but cool nights
Part (b): very little rainfall in the Thar versus cold winters (and wheat) in the plains

questions.q:
A school in Pune is choosing a May tour. Brochure A: sand dunes, scorching days, chilly nights and hardly any rain. Brochure B: a hill resort with mild winters and summers that never get fierce; the journey is six hours by bus. Brochure C: rice fields, spice gardens and a long sea shore. Brochure D: a mountain valley with snowy winters and cool summers; the journey takes two days. An elderly teacher who dislikes long journeys will accompany the group.
(a) Name the climate type of each brochure and the words in it that gave the type away.
(b) Which two brochures are set in cooler highland climates, where people from the plains seek relief from the heat?
(c) Which brochure would be least suitable for a trip in the monsoon months, and why?
(d) Between the two cooler options, which would you recommend for this group? Weigh the climate against the journey.
questions.a: (a) A arid (hardly any rain, scorching days, chilly nights); B temperate (mild winters, summers never fierce); C tropical wet (rice, spices, monsoon-fed); D alpine (snowy winters, cool summers). (b) B and D. (c) C, because it gets heavy rainfall in the monsoon months. (d) Either with reasons: B is cooler than the plains and has a short journey; D's cool summers also give relief but the two-day journey is hard for the elderly teacher. Credit a choice weighing both.
s: Part (a): arid, temperate, tropical wet, alpine with the clue words
Part (b): B and D
Part (c): C, heavy monsoon rainfall
Part (d): a choice weighing climate against the journey

questions.q: The temperate, semi-arid and tropical climates of the chapter all have winters that are moderately cold or mild. Present them in three short lines (winter, summer, rainfall), then say which two are hardest to tell apart from the winter alone and what separates them.
questions.a: Temperate (hills and hill stations): winters moderately cold, summers not too hot. Semi-arid (central Deccan Plateau): hot summers, mild winters, moderate rainfall during the rainy season. Tropical (eastern India and the southern peninsula): a mild winter, distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds. Semi-arid and tropical both have mild winters, so the winter alone cannot separate them; the rainfall pattern does (moderate rainfall in the rainy season versus distinct wet and dry periods under monsoon winds).
s: Temperate described correctly
Semi-arid described correctly
Tropical described correctly
Semi-arid and tropical named as the pair that share a mild winter
Separating feature: rainfall pattern

questions.q: A traveller's note reads, 'This place has snowy winters, extremely hot days and very little rainfall, all in one climate.' Show that this cannot be a single climate type from the chapter.
questions.a: Snowy winters belong to the alpine Himalayas, where summers are cool, so extremely hot days cannot occur there. Extremely hot days with very little rainfall describe the arid Thar, but its nights are cool and the chapter links snowy winters to the Himalayas, not the Thar. No climate in the list combines the three, so the note mixes two climates.
s: Snowy winters assigned to the alpine climate, whose summers are cool
Extremely hot days and very little rainfall assigned to the arid Thar
Conclusion: the three features cannot belong to one climate

questions.q: An entrepreneur plans two shops: one selling the thickest woollens and one selling raincoats and umbrellas, with sales peaking in the monsoon months. (a) Which region of the chapter suits each shop? (b) Why would the raincoat shop do badly in the Thar?
questions.a: (a) Woollens: the Himalayas, with an alpine climate of cold, snowy winters; raincoats: the western coastal strip, which receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon months. (b) The Thar has an arid climate with very little rainfall, so there is little rain to sell raincoats for.
s: Part (a): alpine Himalayas for woollens; western coast for raincoats
Part (b): very little rainfall in the Thar

questions.q: Ravi says, 'The Deccan Plateau is arid like the Thar, because both are dry.' Correct him by naming the Deccan's climate type and one feature in which it differs from the Thar's.
questions.a: The Deccan Plateau is semi-arid, not arid: it has hot summers, mild winters and moderate rainfall during the rainy season, whereas the Thar has extremely hot days, cool nights and very little rainfall.
s: Climate type: semi-arid
A contrast: moderate rainfall (and mild winters) versus very little rainfall (cool nights)

questions.q:
Three travellers write in their diaries. Anil: 'We wore our thickest woollens; snow covered the village in winter and the summer was cool.' Beena: 'Summers were very hot and winters cold; golden wheat covered the fields.' Chetan: 'Rain poured through the monsoon months; our fields grow rice and our gardens grow spices.'
(i) Name the region and the climate each traveller describes.
(ii) Contrast the climate behind Beena's wheat with that behind Chetan's rice.
questions.a: (i) Anil: the Himalayas, alpine climate. Beena: the northern plains, subtropical climate. Chetan: the western coastal strip, tropical wet climate. (ii) Beena's region has very hot summers and cold winters, where most of India's wheat is grown; Chetan's coast receives heavy rainfall in the monsoon months, favourable to rice and spices.
s: Anil: Himalayas and alpine
Beena: northern plains and subtropical
Chetan: western coast and tropical wet
Beena's climate: very hot summers, cold winters
Chetan's climate: heavy monsoon rain

questions.q: Write a three-line riddle (no place names) so that a classmate can identify the semi-arid climate of the Deccan Plateau. Then give its answer.
questions.a: Any riddle using hot summers, mild winters and moderate rainfall during the rainy season, e.g. 'Summers are hot, winters mild; moderate rain falls in the rainy season. Where am I?' Answer: the central Deccan Plateau (semi-arid).
s: Clue on summers and winters
Clue on rainfall, moderate in the rainy season
Correct answer: Deccan Plateau, semi-arid

questions.q:
A family in Nagpur wants a May holiday. The grandfather's doctor says the daily high should not cross 30 degrees C and the night low should not fall below 16, because of his joint pain. Resort H, in the hills at 1,500 m, has May highs of 27 and lows of 14 and costs Rs 14,000 for the family. Resort S is a beach resort at sea level at about the same latitude, with highs of 34 and lows of 26 and costs Rs 9,000. (All figures are invented.)
(a) Which limit does each resort break, and by how many degrees?
(b) Name the factor behind H's lower highs and the factor behind S's warm nights, with the chapter's reason for each.
(c) Work out how much more H costs than S.
(d) Neither resort meets both limits. Which would you choose, and what precaution would you suggest?
questions.a: (a) H breaks the night-low limit by 16 - 14 = 2 degrees; S breaks the high limit by 34 - 30 = 4 degrees. (b) H: altitude, since temperature decreases as height increases (less dense air, farther from the surface heated by the sun). S: nearness to the sea, since the sea loses heat slowly and moderates temperature, so coastal nights stay warm. (c) 14,000 - 9,000 = Rs 5,000. (d) Either, with reasons: H misses by 2 degrees on cold nights, which warm clothing can cover, and costs Rs 5,000 more; S misses by 4 degrees in the daytime heat every day with nothing to cover it. A choice of H with a precaution (warm clothing at night) is better supported; S is acceptable only with an argument about cost and a plan for the afternoon heat.
s: Part (a): H low 2 below the limit; S high 4 above
Part (b): altitude for H; sea moderation for S, each with a reason
Part (c): Rs 5,000
Part (d): a choice weighing limits and cost with a precaution

questions.q: Lekha in Kanniyakumari wears light cotton clothes even in the winter months, while her cousin in Srinagar needs woollens then. Which explanation fits latitude as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: Kanniyakumari is close to the Equator, where the rays are nearly perpendicular and their energy is focused on a small area; Srinagar's rays are more inclined.
o: Kanniyakumari is near the Equator, where the rays are nearly perpendicular and their energy falls on a small area.
Kanniyakumari is at a greater height, where thinner air holds the sun's heat for much longer than at Srinagar.
Kanniyakumari is far from the sea, so the land there loses heat slowly and its winters are never allowed to get cold.
Srinagar gets more perpendicular rays than Kanniyakumari, so its energy is focused on a smaller area of ground.

questions.q: Two towns lie at the same latitude. Beltola has a summer high of 41 and a winter low of 8 degrees C. Chandpur has a summer high of 33 and a winter low of 21 degrees C (all figures invented). The town nearer the sea is ___.
questions.a: Chandpur

questions.q: A geography group records the January noon temperature of four towns on the coast, all at sea level: Town A (8 N) 29 degrees C, Town B (15 N) 27, Town C (24 N) 21, Town D (32 N) 14. Which conclusion does this table support best?
questions.a: All four are coastal and at sea level, so only latitude changes. Temperature falls from 29 to 14 degrees C as latitude increases because the sun's rays become oblique and spread over a larger surface.
o: With height and the sea held the same, temperature falls as latitude rises, since rays become more oblique and spread out.
With height and the sea held the same, temperature rises as latitude rises, since rays become more perpendicular and focused.
Height explains the fall in temperature from A to D, since the towns at higher latitude stand on higher ground.
Distance from the sea explains the fall from A to D, since the towns at higher latitude are farther inland.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ooty is cooler than Coimbatore although the two lie at almost the same latitude.
Reason (R): Temperature decreases as altitude increases, because the air becomes less dense and is farther from the surface heated by the sun.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true; Ooty is a high hill station and R gives the chapter's explanation of why height cools a place.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: The chapter gives the summer temperatures of Ooty as 10 to 25 degrees C and of Coimbatore, at almost the same latitude, as 25 to 38. (a) By how many degrees do their lowest and their highest summer temperatures differ? (b) Why can latitude not explain the difference, and which factor does?
questions.a: (a) Lowest: 25 - 10 = 15 degrees C; highest: 38 - 25 = 13 degrees C. (b) The latitudes are almost the same, so latitude cannot be the cause; Ooty is a hill station at a much greater height, and temperature decreases as altitude increases.
s: Part (a): 15 and 13 degrees C
Part (b): same latitude, so altitude is the factor

questions.q:
Match each pair of places in Column A with the explanation in Column B (all figures and places are invented for practice).
Column A: 1. Two towns, both 300 km inland and 20 m above sea level, at 10 N and 30 N, have very different winters.  2. Two towns at 12 N, both 300 km inland, stand at 20 m and 1,900 m and have very different summers.  3. Two towns at 12 N and 20 m, one on the coast and one 300 km inland, have different temperature ranges.  4. Town P (8 N, 20 m, on the coast) and Town Q (34 N, 1,800 m, 400 km inland) have very different climates.
Column B: a. latitude  b. altitude  c. nearness to the sea  d. all three factors acting together
questions.a: 1-a (only latitude differs), 2-b (only height differs), 3-c (only nearness to the sea differs), 4-d (latitude, height and distance from the sea all differ).

questions.q: Town M is on the coast with a summer high of 31 and a winter low of 19 degrees C. Town N lies inland at the same latitude, with 42 and 7. A pupil says, 'M is cooler than N all through the year.' Which verdict agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: 31 is below 42, so M is cooler in summer; 19 is above 7, so M is warmer in winter. The sea keeps coastal summers from being too hot and winters from being too cold.
o: Partly right: M is cooler in summer (31 against 42) but warmer in winter (19 against 7), as the sea moderates temperature.
Fully right: M is cooler in summer (31 against 42) and in winter (19 against 7), as sea air always cools the coast.
Fully wrong: M is warmer in summer (31 against 42) and in winter (19 against 7), as the sea always heats the coast.
Partly right: M is cooler in winter (19 against 7) but warmer in summer (31 against 42), as the sea moderates temperature.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Near the Equator the sun's rays are oblique, so their heat spreads over a larger area.
2. The sea acts as a moderator, so coastal summers are not too hot and winters not too cold.
3. Two places at the same latitude must have the same temperature range.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: rays are nearly perpendicular at the Equator. 3 is false: Mumbai (range about 14) and Nagpur (about 34) are at a similar latitude. 2 is correct.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Mahesh says, 'Climbing a mountain and travelling from Kanniyakumari to Srinagar make a place cooler for the very same reason.' Do you agree? Give the cause in each case.
questions.a: No. Going north, higher latitude makes the sun's rays oblique, so their energy spreads over a larger surface and passes through more atmosphere. Going up a mountain, the air becomes less dense and is farther from the surface the sun heats. The causes are different.
s: Verdict: disagrees, the causes differ
Latitude: oblique rays spread out; altitude: less dense air, farther from heated surface

questions.q: Aman records the midday temperature on the same day in two places that lie at almost the same latitude: Mahabaleshwar, a hill station, 26 degrees C, and a town on the plains below it, 37 degrees C. Which factor explains the difference best?
questions.a: The latitudes are almost the same, so latitude cannot be the cause. The hill station is much higher and temperature decreases with altitude.
o: Altitude, since Mahabaleshwar is a hill station.
Latitude, since the two towns are at different distances from the Equator.
Wind, since hill stations receive only cold winds.
Proximity to the sea, since the hill station is on the coast.

questions.q: Near the Equator a beam of sunlight carrying 600 units of energy falls on 100 square km of ground. An identical beam falls on 250 square km of ground near a pole (the figures are invented). (a) Find the energy received per square km at each place. (b) Apart from this, give the other reason the chapter offers for the pole receiving less heat.
questions.a: (a) Equator: 600 / 100 = 6 units per sq km; pole: 600 / 250 = 2.4 units per sq km. (b) The inclined rays also have to pass through more of the Earth's atmosphere, which further dissipates their energy.
s: Part (a): 6 and 2.4 units per sq km
Part (b): rays pass through more atmosphere

questions.q: Fig. 3.6 of the chapter shows that land absorbs and loses heat quickly while the sea absorbs and loses it slowly. Using this, explain (a) why a seaside town is cooler than an inland town at the same latitude in summer, and (b) why it is warmer in winter.
questions.a: (a) In summer the land heats up quickly, so inland places get very hot, while the sea heats slowly and cools the coastal air, so seaside summers are not too hot. (b) In winter the land loses heat rapidly, so inland places turn cold, while the sea loses heat slowly and warms the coastal air, so seaside winters are not too cold.
s: Summer: land heats quickly, sea slowly, coast cooled by sea air
Winter: land loses heat rapidly, sea slowly, coast warmed by sea air

questions.q: Alibag lies on the coast with a summer high of 33 and a winter low of 21 degrees C. Satara, at about the same latitude but inland, has 41 and 12 (these figures are invented for practice). (a) Find the range of temperature of each town. (b) Which factor explains the difference in their ranges, and what does it do to coastal summers and winters?
questions.a: (a) Alibag 33 - 21 = 12 degrees C; Satara 41 - 12 = 29 degrees C. (b) Nearness to the sea, which acts as a moderator: coastal summers are not too hot and winters not too cold.
s: Part (a): 12 and 29 degrees C
Part (b): the sea as moderator, cooler summers and milder winters

questions.q: Meera compares a hill town H (May daily low 8 and high 22 degrees C) with a plains town P at almost the same latitude (May daily low 22 and high 36 degrees C). She says, 'H is cooler, but its range of temperature is the same as P's.' Check her claim.
questions.a: H: 22 - 8 = 14 degrees C. P: 36 - 22 = 14 degrees C. The ranges are equal, so Meera is right. H is cooler because of its altitude, but being cooler does not by itself change the gap between the highest and lowest values.
s: Both ranges correct: 14 and 14
Verdict: Meera is right
Reason: altitude lowers the level of temperatures, range is maximum minus minimum

questions.q: A table gives invented figures for three towns. Town A: latitude 11 N, height 20 m, 3 km from the sea, summer high 33, winter low 22. Town B: latitude 11 N, height 1,800 m, 90 km from the sea, summer high 22, winter low 8. Town C: latitude 33 N, height 1,600 m, 400 km from the sea, summer high 24, winter low 1 (all in degrees C). (i) Find the range of each town. (ii) Which factor explains why B's summer is so much cooler than A's? (iii) Why is A's range the smallest? (iv) Give two factors that make C the coldest in winter.
questions.a: (i) A 33 - 22 = 11; B 22 - 8 = 14; C 24 - 1 = 23 degrees C. (ii) Altitude: B is much higher at the same latitude. (iii) A is close to the sea, which moderates temperature. (iv) C lies at a higher latitude (farther from the Equator) and is high and far from the sea.
s: Ranges 11, 14 and 23
B cooler than A: altitude
A's small range: nearness to the sea
C coldest: higher latitude
C coldest: a second factor such as height or distance from the sea

questions.q: Three towns A, B and C are all 300 km inland (all figures are invented). Town A lies at a height of 10 m. Town B lies at the same latitude as A but at 1,400 m. Town C lies at the same height as A (10 m) but far to the north of it. Which single factor mainly explains the difference between A and B, and which single factor explains the difference between A and C? Give the chapter's reason for each.
questions.a: A and B: altitude, because B is much higher at the same latitude and the same distance from the sea, and temperature decreases with altitude (the air is less dense and farther from the surface the sun heats). A and C: latitude, because C is farther from the Equator, so the sun's rays are more inclined and their energy spreads over a larger surface.
s: A and B: altitude named
A and C: latitude named
A chapter reason for each factor

questions.q: Make up summer-high and winter-low figures (in degrees C) for two towns at the same latitude, one on the coast and one far inland, so that they show the sea acting as a moderator. Work out each town's range and state in one line what your figures show.
questions.a: Any valid figures in which the coastal town has the lower summer high, the higher winter low and therefore the smaller range, e.g. coastal 32 and 18 (range 14), inland 44 and 10 (range 34). The figures show that near the sea summers are not too hot and winters not too cold, while inland temperatures are more extreme.
s: Coastal: lower summer high and higher winter low than inland
Both ranges computed correctly from the figures given
Conclusion: sea moderates, inland is more extreme

questions.q:
Three towns in the same part of Maharashtra lie at about the same latitude (all figures are invented). Town P is 10 m above sea level and 2 km from the sea, with a summer high of 33 degrees C and a winter low of 20. Town Q is 10 m above sea level and 300 km from the sea, with 43 and 9. Town R is 1,400 m above sea level and 300 km from the sea, with 27 and 8. A school wants one town for two camps, one in May and one in January.
(a) Find the range of temperature of each town.
(b) By how many degrees is P's summer high below Q's, and its winter low above Q's? Which factor accounts for both gaps, and how?
(c) Q and R are equally far from the sea, and R's summer high is far below Q's. Name the factor and give one reason from the chapter.
(d) Which town would you recommend for both camps, and what would you tell the parents?
questions.a: (a) P 33 - 20 = 13; Q 43 - 9 = 34; R 27 - 8 = 19 degrees C. (b) P's summer high is 43 - 33 = 10 degrees below Q's, and its winter low is 20 - 9 = 11 degrees above Q's; nearness to the sea explains both, because the sea moderates temperature. (c) Altitude: temperature decreases with height because the air is less dense and is farther from the surface heated by the sun. (d) P is the safer choice since it never rises above 33 or falls below 20. R is 16 degrees cooler than Q in May (43 - 27) but its January low of 8 needs warm clothing; Q is the hottest in May and cold in January (9). Credit a choice with a reason from the data.
s: Part (a): ranges 13, 34 and 19
Part (b): gaps 10 and 11, the sea as moderator
Part (c): altitude with a reason
Part (d): recommendation backed by the temperature data

questions.q:
A traveller writes: 'Day 1 at Kanniyakumari, at sea level near the Equator: warm even at night. Day 2 at a hill station H in the south, at the same latitude as Kanniyakumari but 1,600 m high: I needed a sweater. Day 3 at Srinagar, far to the north: colder still.'
(i) Which factor keeps Kanniyakumari warm almost all year?
(ii) Give two reasons from the chapter why H is cooler than Kanniyakumari at the same latitude.
(iii) Explain how latitude, not height, would make Srinagar cooler than Kanniyakumari.
questions.a: (i) Low latitude: close to the Equator the rays are nearly perpendicular and their energy is focused on a small area. (ii) The atmospheric pressure and air density decrease with height, and less dense air is cooler; and H is farther from the surface heated by the sun, so the air is less hot. (iii) At Srinagar's higher latitude the rays are inclined, so their energy is spread over a larger surface and passes through more atmosphere, so Srinagar gets less heat.
s: (i) low latitude with perpendicular, focused rays
(ii) reason 1: pressure and density fall with height, so the air is cooler
(ii) reason 2: farther from the surface heated by the sun
(iii) rays inclined and spread over a larger surface
(iii) pass through more atmosphere, so less heat

questions.q: A survey team records the following. Which one is a microclimate in the chapter's sense?
questions.a: A microclimate is a climate localised in a small area that differs from the surrounding region; forests and enclosed valleys are examples. The plateau's climate covers a large region, a heat wave is weather, and the monsoon rain covers the subcontinent.
o: A 6-hectare forest patch that stays cooler and more humid than the farmland around it
The semi-arid climate that the whole central Deccan Plateau has, with hot summers and mild winters
A three-day heat wave that covered Punjab and Haryana when hot western winds blew in May
The summer rainfall that falls across the whole subcontinent when winds blow from ocean to land

questions.q: Pinky says, 'Winds can change only how hot or cold a place is; they cannot change how moist the air is or whether it rains.' Which example from the chapter shows she is wrong?
questions.a: Pinky is wrong because winds affect humidity too, and in turn precipitation: the chapter contrasts dry winds from distant deserts with winds from the sea that bring moisture and may bring rain. The other options describe temperature only.
o: Winds coming from the sea bring moisture over the land, which may result in rainfall.
Winds from the west cause severe heat waves in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh in summer.
Cold winds from across the Himalayas creep into the foothills and cause cold waves in winter.
Winds from the west carry hot air over the deserts of Arabia and on to Afghanistan.

questions.q:
Kheda is a village in an enclosed valley; Sundarpur is an open plain town 20 km away. Thirty years of records show summer highs of 38 degrees C at Kheda and 43 at Sundarpur, and winter lows of 3 at Kheda and 9 at Sundarpur (invented figures). A hospital trust wants a year-round rest centre for elderly patients who suffer from heat stress in summer and from cold in winter. Kheda is reached by a 3-hour mountain road; Sundarpur has a district hospital 2 km away.
(a) Is the Kheda-Sundarpur difference weather or microclimate? Name two facts in the stem that decide it.
(b) By how much do the summer highs differ, and by how much do the winter lows differ?
(c) What do these gaps say about each place for patients who suffer in both seasons?
(d) Which place would you choose? Give an advantage and a drawback of your choice.
questions.a: (a) A microclimate: an enclosed valley is a small area with a climate that differs from its surroundings, and thirty years of records show a lasting pattern, not one day's weather. (b) Summer: 43 - 38 = 5 degrees C; winter: 9 - 3 = 6 degrees C. (c) Kheda is 5 degrees cooler in summer, which helps against heat stress, but 6 degrees colder in winter, which worsens the cold; Sundarpur is the reverse. (d) Either with reasons: Kheda relieves summer heat but is colder in winter and a 3-hour road from medical help; Sundarpur is milder in winter with a hospital 2 km away but hotter in summer. Credit a choice with an advantage and a drawback taken from the data.
s: Part (a): microclimate, with two decisive facts
Part (b): 5 and 6 degrees C
Part (c): Kheda cooler in summer but colder in winter, Sundarpur the reverse
Part (d): a choice with advantage and drawback

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The nearly flat Thar has nothing to protect it from hot and dry winds.
Reason (R): The Himalayas and the Karakoram protect the whole Thar from every wind that blows towards India.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: the Himalayas and Karakoram protect the subcontinent only to some extent, and only from the cold winds of Central Asia, not from every wind.

questions.q: On a May morning a moist wind blows in from the sea over a coastal town, yet no rain falls that day. A pupil says this contradicts the chapter. Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says winds from the sea bring moisture over the land, which may result in rainfall. 'May' means rain is possible, not guaranteed.
o: It does not: sea winds bring moisture over the land, which may result in rainfall, but not certainly.
It does: sea winds always bring moisture and the chapter says moisture always results in rainfall.
It does not: winds from the sea are dry, so the town could never expect rain from them on any day.
It does: the chapter says only winds from the west can cause rainfall, so a sea wind cannot.

questions.q: At 2 pm in June a weather team reads 41 degrees C in a crowded concrete market square, 37 at a park 3 km away and 36 in villages 15 km away. The team suspects the market has a microclimate. Which further fact from the chapter would best support this?
questions.a: An urban heat island forms in a city with a large number of buildings and other concrete structures and very little vegetation, which trap heat, so it is much warmer than the surrounding region.
o: The market has a very large number of buildings and concrete structures and very little vegetation.
The villages lie in the same state as the market and are reached by the same hot western wind.
The market square is bigger than the park, so its temperature cannot be compared with the park's.
The market's reading was taken at 2 pm, so it shows the weather and says nothing about climate.

questions.q: A team notes three things: (i) the market square of a large city is 4 degrees warmer than villages around it, year after year; (ii) a dry, hot wind blew across Rajasthan for three afternoons last May; (iii) a forested hollow stays cooler and more humid than the open land around it, year after year. Which of these are microclimates and which is a wind-borne event? Give one reason for each.
questions.a: (i) A microclimate, an urban heat island: many buildings and concrete structures with very little vegetation trap heat, and the gap persists over years. (ii) Not a microclimate: it is a heat wave caused by hot dry winds from the west, a short-lived event over a wide area. (iii) A microclimate: forests are named as having micro-climates of their own, localised in a small area.
s: (i) microclimate (heat island) with its cause
(ii) heat wave from winds, not localised or long-lasting
(iii) microclimate (forest) with a reason

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with what explains it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Dry, scorching air reaches Madhya Pradesh from the west in May.  2. A concrete-heavy market is 4 degrees warmer than villages 15 km away.  3. A desert plain with nothing to shield it is open to hot winds.  4. Sea winds bring showers to a coastal district.
Column B: a. winds that crossed the deserts of Arabia and Afghanistan  b. an urban heat island, a kind of microclimate  c. the nearly flat topography  d. moisture carried by winds from the sea

Read the statements.
1. Winds can change a place's humidity as well as its temperature, because winds from distant deserts are dry and winds from the sea bring moisture.
2. A microclimate must cover an entire state before it can be called one.
3. An enclosed valley cannot have a climate different from the region around it.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
questions.a: Only 1 is correct. 2 is false: a microclimate is localised in a small area. 3 is false: enclosed valleys and some forests have microclimates of their own.

questions.q: Meena says, 'The Thar is dry and hot because the Himalayas do not shield it.' Judge her reasoning using what the chapter says about topography.
questions.a: Not correct as stated. The Himalayas and Karakoram protect, to some extent, the subcontinent from the cold winds of Central Asia, not from hot winds. The Thar's nearly flat topography has nothing to protect it from hot and dry winds; the missing protection is from its own flat land, not from the Himalayas.
s: Verdict: her reason is not correct, since the Himalayas shield from cold winds
The flat topography of the Thar leaves it open to hot, dry winds

questions.q: True or False: 'A busy city centre and the villages around it can lie under the same wind and still differ in temperature by several degrees, because the city can have a microclimate of its own.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A city with a large number of buildings and other concrete structures and very little vegetation traps heat and becomes an urban heat island, often much warmer than the surrounding region, though both lie under the same winds.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: concrete and little vegetation trap heat, giving the city its own microclimate

questions.q: The market square of a city read 41 degrees C and villages 15 km away read 37 on one June afternoon. (a) By how many degrees was the market warmer? (b) A councillor says this single reading proves the market has its own microclimate. What else would the pattern need, going by the chapter's definition of climate?
questions.a: (a) 41 - 37 = 4 degrees C. (b) One afternoon is weather. A microclimate is a climate, a pattern of temperature and humidity in a small area over a long period (three decades or more, as for any climate), so the gap must show up repeatedly in records over many years.
s: Part (a): 4 degrees C
Part (b): a long-term pattern, not one reading

questions.q: Decide whether each is a microclimate in the chapter's sense, and give a reason: (a) the semi-arid climate of the whole central Deccan Plateau; (b) a city with a large number of buildings, concrete structures and very little vegetation.
questions.a: (a) No: it is the climate of a large region, not one localised in a small area. (b) Yes: such an urban heat island traps heat and is much warmer than the surrounding region, so it has a climate of its own in a small area.
s: Part (a): not a microclimate, because it covers a large region
Part (b): yes, an urban heat island differs from its surroundings in a small area

questions.q: Using the chapter's account of winds and the Class 6 water-cycle line it quotes, which sequence explains how a wind from the sea can end in rainfall?
questions.a: The quoted water cycle: water from the ocean and the Earth's surface evaporates as vapour and returns as rain, hail or snow. Winds from the sea carry that moisture over the land, where it may result in rain.
o: Water evaporates from the sea as vapour; the wind carries the moist air over land; the moisture may return as rain.
Water evaporates from the land as vapour; the wind carries the dry air out to sea; the moisture may return as rain.
Water evaporates from the sea as vapour; the wind blows it away from the land; the moisture returns as heat.
Water freezes over the sea as ice; the wind carries it over land; the ice returns as hot dry air.

questions.q: Compare the hot westerly wind that reaches Rajasthan in summer with a wind blowing in from the sea. For each, state the route it travels and what that route does to the air it carries.
questions.a: The westerly wind travels over the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan, so it carries dry, hot air and brings severe heat waves. The sea wind travels over the sea, so it carries moisture over the land, which may result in rainfall.
s: Westerly: desert route, dry and hot air
Sea wind: sea route, moist air that may bring rain

questions.q: Mira says, 'The Himalayas and Karakoram protect the subcontinent only to some extent, so cold winds can still creep into the foothills in winter and cause cold waves.' Do you agree? Support your answer from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the Himalayas and Karakoram protect, to some extent, the subcontinent from the cold winds of Central Asia, which means the protection is partial. It also says that in winter cold winds from across the Himalayas creep into the Himalayan foothills and cause cold waves, which shows the protection is not complete.
s: Verdict: agrees
Protection is only to some extent (Himalayas and Karakoram, cold winds of Central Asia)
Cold winds still creep into the foothills and cause cold waves

questions.q:
A bulletin lists four stations (the figures are invented). Station 1, a flat desert plain, May noon: wind from the west, 46 degrees C, humidity 12 percent. Station 2, a coastal town, May noon: wind from the sea, 31 degrees C, humidity 82 percent. Station 3, a Himalayan foothill town, January dawn: wind from across the Himalayas, 4 degrees C. Station 4, a hill-ringed valley village, January dawn: 8 degrees C, while open land 20 km away records 5.
(i) Explain Station 1's heat and low humidity from the route its wind has travelled.
(ii) By how many degrees is Station 1 hotter than Station 2, and why does Station 2 have so much more moisture in the air?
(iii) Name the kind of event at Station 3 and the wind behind it.
(iv) Which station may have a microclimate, and what further evidence would make you sure?
questions.a: (i) Winds from the west have travelled over the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan, so they bring dry, hot air and heat waves. (ii) 46 - 31 = 15 degrees C; winds from the sea bring moisture over the land, which may result in rainfall. (iii) A cold wave, caused by cold winds from across the Himalayas that creep into the foothills in winter. (iv) Station 4, an enclosed valley that differs from the open land around it; records over many years (a pattern, not one dawn) would confirm it.
s: (i) desert route gives dry, hot air
(ii) 15 degrees C and moisture carried by sea winds
(iii) cold wave from cold winds across the Himalayas
(iv) Station 4 identified as an enclosed valley
(iv) long-term records needed to confirm

questions.q: A city has many concrete buildings and almost no vegetation. Suggest three changes that could reduce its heat, and link each to a cause named in the chapter.
questions.a: Plant more trees and gardens (the city has very little vegetation); reduce the concentration of concrete structures or leave open spaces (many buildings and concrete structures trap heat); provide green areas near buildings. Credit three sensible changes each tied to the causes: many buildings, concrete structures and little vegetation. (Credit is for changes tied to a named cause, not for a fixed list.)
s: First change linked to a cause
Second change linked to a cause
Third change linked to a cause

questions.q:
In June a city bulletin gives noon readings. Place X, a town in the flat Thar, 46 degrees C. Place Y, a Himalayan foothill town, 28 degrees C. Place Z, the busiest part of a large city, 41 degrees C, while villages 15 km away stand at 37. The city has funds for cooling shelters at only one site: Z's central market (about 300 outdoor workers) or the suburb next to the village belt (about 900 outdoor workers, at 37 degrees C).
(a) Which winds are the main cause of X's heat, and how do they become hot and dry?
(b) Why is Z hotter than the villages?
(c) Which feature of X's topography leaves it open to the hot, dry wind, and by how many degrees is X hotter than Y?
(d) Which site would you choose for the shelters? Weigh the heat difference against the numbers.
questions.a: (a) Winds from the west that travelled over the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan, picking up dry, hot air. (b) Z is an urban heat island: many buildings and concrete structures with very little vegetation trap heat. (c) X is nearly flat, so nothing protects it from hot and dry winds; 46 - 28 = 18 degrees C hotter than Y. (d) Either with reasons: the market is 4 degrees hotter (41 - 37) but has only 300 workers; the suburb has 900, three times as many, at 37 degrees C. A strong answer weighs both the heat and the numbers (heat per worker versus numbers helped).
s: Part (a): western winds over deserts bring dry hot air
Part (b): urban heat island, concrete buildings and little vegetation
Part (c): flat terrain leaves X unprotected; 18 degrees C difference
Part (d): shelter site chosen with the numbers weighed

questions.q:
A student writes in the school magazine: 'In May our relatives in Jaipur suffered a heat wave. In my city, the old market, where it read 41 degrees C at noon, always feels hotter than the villages we pass on the way, which read 37.'
(i) Name the wind behind the heat wave and describe where it has travelled.
(ii) Name the effect that makes the market warmer than the villages, give two causes of it, and say by how much it was warmer.
(iii) Explain why the flat desert is more exposed to the heat wave winds than a region behind the Himalayas is to cold ones.
questions.a: (i) Winds from the west that have travelled over the deserts of Arabia to Afghanistan, bringing dry and hot air. (ii) An urban heat island, a microclimate, caused by a large number of buildings and concrete structures and very little vegetation, which trap heat; it was 41 - 37 = 4 degrees C warmer. (iii) The nearly flat Thar has nothing to protect it from hot and dry winds, whereas the Himalayas and Karakoram protect, to some extent, the subcontinent from the cold winds of Central Asia.
s: Western winds, hot and dry, and the route over Arabia and Afghanistan
Urban heat island named with two causes
Difference of 4 degrees C
Flat Thar exposed versus mountains shielding to some extent

questions.q: The chapter says the word 'southwest' in southwest monsoon reflects the direction the winds come from. A pupil uses the same rule on the winter monsoon, which is called the northeast monsoon. Which statement follows?
questions.a: By the chapter's rule the name gives the direction the winds come from, so they come from the northeast. In winter the pattern reverses and winds blow from land to ocean.
o: Its winds come from the northeast, blowing from the cooling land towards the ocean.
Its winds go towards the northeast, blowing from the ocean towards the heated land.
Its winds come from the northeast, blowing from the heated ocean towards the land.
Its winds go towards the northeast, blowing from the cooling land towards the ocean.

questions.q:
The science club of a school in southern India records that the Golden Shower tree blossomed on 12 April this year. The village headman asks for a forecast, because farmers must decide whether to sow on the date the saying predicts or wait for the first rains. Last year the tree blossomed on 10 April, but the rains reached the village only on 15 June. If farmers sow early and the rains come on time, they gain Rs 12,000 of extra yield; if they sow early and the rains come late, they lose seed worth Rs 30,000. (All money figures are invented.)
(a) By what date does the saying (50 days) predict the rains this year?
(b) By how many days did last year's rains miss the saying's date?
(c) What chance of the saying being right would make early sowing worth the risk, on average?
(d) Should the club advise sowing early or waiting? Justify with your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 12 April + 50 days = 1 June. (b) 10 April + 50 days = 30 May; the rains came on 15 June, so 16 days late. (c) Early sowing pays on average if p x 12,000 > (1 - p) x 30,000, that is p > 30,000 / 42,000, about 71 percent. (d) Credit either with reasons: waiting is safer because last year's saying missed by 16 days and the chapter treats such sayings as traditional knowledge to preserve, not as a precise forecast, and the advance of the rains is not smooth; sowing early is defensible only if the club has other evidence that the saying is right more than about 71 percent of the time.
s: Part (a): 1 June
Part (b): 16 days late
Part (c): about 71 percent break-even
Part (d): a decision tied to the break-even chance and last year's miss

questions.q: A weather group logs sea-level pressure (hPa) for the Asian landmass and the nearby ocean. In May: land 996, ocean 1008. In December: land 1022, ocean 1011. Using the chapter's rule about pressure and wind, which pair of wind directions follows?
questions.a: Air flows from high to low pressure. In May the ocean (1008) is higher than the land (996), so winds blow from ocean to land with moisture; in December the land (1022) is higher than the ocean (1011), so winds blow from land to ocean and are dry.
o: May: ocean to land, bringing moist air; December: land to ocean, bringing dry air
May: land to ocean, bringing dry air; December: ocean to land, bringing moist air
May: ocean to land, bringing moist air; December: ocean to land, bringing moist air
May: land to ocean, bringing dry air; December: land to ocean, bringing dry air

questions.q: Tara says, 'In winter the winds blow from land to ocean and are dry, so no part of India gets any rain from the monsoon in winter.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The winter winds are mostly dry and blow from land to ocean, but a part of them passes over the Bay of Bengal, collects some moisture and brings rainfall to parts of east and south India. This is the winter or northeast monsoon.
s: Verdict: not right
Part of the winds crosses the Bay of Bengal and gathers moisture
Rain falls in parts of east and south India (northeast monsoon)

questions.q: In a village in southern India the Golden Shower tree starts to blossom on 15 April. Using the saying that the monsoon arrives within 50 days of the blossoming, by what date at the latest should the village expect it?
questions.a: 15 April + 50 days = 4 June (15 days left in April, 31 in May, 4 in June). 15 May is 30 days, 30 May is 45 days and 14 June is 60 days.
o: 15 May
30 May
4 June
14 June

questions.q: In winter the Asian landmass loses heat faster than the ocean, so the air pressure over the land becomes ___ than the pressure over the ocean, and the monsoon winds blow from land to ocean.
questions.a: higher

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. In summer the Asian landmass heats up faster than the ocean, which is why moist winds are drawn from the ocean towards the land.
2. In winter the winds from the land are dry on the whole, yet some of them bring rain to parts of east and south India.
3. The summer monsoon reaches every part of India in the first week of June.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: 1 and 2 are correct. 3 is false: the rains start at the southern tip in early June and take several weeks, until mid-July, to cover the whole subcontinent.

questions.q: A headline reads 'The monsoon arrived in Kochi on 4 June with a heavy downpour.' (a) Strictly speaking, what does the word 'monsoon' refer to? (b) Why do people nevertheless use it for the rain?
questions.a: (a) Seasonal winds over a large area of the Indian Ocean and surrounding regions (from the Arabic mausim, 'season'). (b) The ocean winds carry moisture that condenses over the warmer land and falls as heavy rain, so 'monsoon' commonly refers to the seasonal rains.
s: Part (a): seasonal winds (mausim means season)
Part (b): moisture-laden winds bring the rains, so the word is used for the rains

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with the idea in Column B that explains it.
Column A: 1. Pressure over the land reads lower than over the ocean in May, and rain-bearing winds blow inland.  2. A range of hills gives its west side heavy rain and the plateau behind it little.  3. Fishermen see fish that stay under water rise to the surface and expect the rains.  4. Dry December winds that cross the Bay of Bengal bring showers to parts of south India.
Column B: a. a natural barrier, the Western Ghats  b. the winter or northeast monsoon  c. traditional local knowledge  d. low pressure over the heated landmass

Assertion (A): In summer, the monsoon winds blow from the land towards the ocean.
Reason (R): Air flows from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure.
Choose the correct option.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
questions.a: A is false: in summer the heated land has low pressure, so winds are drawn from the cooler ocean towards the land. R is true, and it is the rule that gives the correct direction.

questions.q: In July, Town P on the western slopes of a range of hills records 2,400 mm of rain this year, while Town Q, on the plateau to the east at the same latitude, records 300 mm with long breaks. Which idea from the chapter fits these records best?
questions.a: The chapter says the Western Ghats act as a natural barrier: their western slopes receive much rainfall while the Deccan plateau to the east receives less, often with interruptions.
o: A natural barrier, like the Western Ghats, gives the west slopes much rain and the plateau less, with interruptions.
The northeast monsoon, which blows from land to ocean in July, gives the plateau its rain and leaves the west slopes dry.
The land cools faster than the ocean in July, which lowers the pressure over the plateau and brings it heavy rain.
The rains start in the north and move south, so the west slopes get their rain late and the plateau gets it first.

questions.q: A hostel warden says, 'In summer the winds blow from the ocean towards the land because the ocean is hot and the land is cool.' (a) Correct the statement using the chapter. (b) Name the property of land and ocean that drives the monsoon.
questions.a: (a) In summer the Asian landmass heats up and forms a powerful low-pressure system; the cooler ocean has higher pressure, so winds are drawn from the ocean to the land. (b) Land heats up or cools down faster than the ocean.
s: Part (a): land is hot, ocean cooler; low pressure over land draws the winds
Part (b): land heats and cools faster than the ocean

questions.q: A student reports: 'Pressure over the Asian landmass is 1022 hPa and over the ocean 1011 hPa; winds are blowing from the ocean to the land bringing heavy monsoon rain.' Show that these readings and this wind direction cannot be true together.
questions.a: Air always flows from high pressure to low pressure. Land at 1022 hPa has higher pressure than the ocean at 1011 hPa, so winds would blow from the land to the ocean, and dry ones at that, as in the winter pattern. Winds from the ocean to the land with heavy rain need the opposite readings, with lower pressure over the land.
s: States the rule: air flows from high to low pressure
Applies it: land is higher, so wind blows from land to ocean
Concludes that moist ocean-to-land winds need low pressure over land

questions.q:
Town A lies on the western slopes of the Western Ghats and receives about 3,000 mm of rain a year. Town B lies on the Deccan Plateau east of the Ghats and receives about 600 mm, with long breaks in the rainy season (invented figures). A farmers' society in Town B has Rs 6 lakh and can use it for only one plan. Plan 1: a village tank that stores water for the breaks. Plan 2: bringing three times as much land under a rain-fed crop sown in early June, which pays well in a year of good rains and fails if breaks are long.
(a) Which natural feature explains the difference between A and B, and which wind does it meet?
(b) How many times as much rain does A receive as B, and how many millimetres more?
(c) What does the chapter say about the rain pattern east of the Ghats, and why does it matter for Plan 2?
(d) Which plan would you recommend? Justify using the rainfall data.
questions.a: (a) The Western Ghats act as a natural barrier to the southwest monsoon winds. (b) 3000 / 600 = 5 times, which is 3000 - 600 = 2400 mm more. (c) The Deccan Plateau receives less rain, often with interruptions; interruptions can wither a rain-fed crop. (d) Either with reasons: Plan 1 protects against the interruptions; Plan 2 gives higher returns if the rains are good but risks the whole crop on 600 mm with breaks. Credit a choice weighing returns against the risk.
s: Part (a): the Western Ghats as barrier
Part (b): 5 times, 2400 mm more
Part (c): less rain with interruptions, so rain-fed crops are at risk
Part (d): recommendation weighing return and risk

questions.q: A report says the summer rains reached the southern tip of India on 9 June and covered the whole subcontinent on 12 July of the same year. (a) For how many days did the advance last? (b) Why should a farmer on the Deccan Plateau not expect steady rain during it?
questions.a: (a) 9 June to 12 July = 21 days left in June + 12 in July = 33 days. (b) The advance is not smooth: the Western Ghats act as a natural barrier, so their western slopes get much rain while the Deccan plateau to the east receives less, often with interruptions.
s: Part (a): 33 days
Part (b): Ghats barrier; Deccan gets less rain with interruptions

questions.q:
A school records the dates (same year, invented) on which the summer rains reached four places: City P, at the southern tip, 4 June; City Q, 18 June; City R, 2 July; and the last part of the subcontinent, 16 July.
(i) Find the number of days between successive dates.
(ii) What does the sequence of dates show about the direction of the advance, and how does it compare with the chapter's dates?
(iii) A student says, 'The equal gaps prove that the rains advance smoothly.' Evaluate this using the chapter.
questions.a: (i) 4 to 18 June = 14 days; 18 June to 2 July = 14 days; 2 to 16 July = 14 days (42 days in all). (ii) The rains advance northward from the southern tip, as the chapter says, starting in early June and covering the subcontinent by mid-July. (iii) The student is wrong: four dates say when rain first arrived, not how steady it was. The chapter says the progression is not smooth: the Western Ghats act as a barrier, with the Deccan plateau getting less rain and often with interruptions.
s: Part (i): 14, 14 and 14 days
Part (ii): northward advance, early June to mid-July
Part (iii): dates of first arrival say nothing about interruptions
Part (iii): the Ghats barrier and the Deccan interruptions cited

questions.q: Two traditional signs are quoted in the chapter: Konkan fishermen see fishes that normally stay under water at the surface, and crows build their nests high on tree-tops. (a) Which sign is used to predict the onset of the monsoon and which the amount of rain? (b) This year fishes are seen at the surface and crows have built their nests low. What do the two signs suggest together?
questions.a: (a) The fishes at the surface are taken as a sign that the monsoon is about to begin (onset); the height of the crows' nests is linked to the amount of rain. (b) The monsoon is about to begin, and low nests suggest that the rainfall is likely to be heavy.
