s: Part (a): fishes for the onset, crows' nests for the amount of rain
Part (b): onset is near and rainfall is likely to be heavy

questions.q: Read this answer: 'Fish that normally stay under water were seen at the surface, so the fishermen expected the monsoon to start.' Write the question to which it responds, and say why the chapter wants such knowledge preserved.
questions.a: Question: How do fishermen on the Konkan coast predict the onset of the monsoon? The chapter calls such local traditional knowledge, built through careful observation of nature and experience over generations, an important heritage that must be preserved.
s: A suitable question about the Konkan fishermen and the monsoon
Notes it is traditional knowledge from careful observation
Says it is a heritage we must preserve

questions.q: A student says, 'The monsoon matters only to farmers.' Use two items from the chapter that are not about crops to show she is wrong.
questions.a: The chapter says that during the monsoon months the rivers fill up, the soil is soaked with water and life thrives, so the monsoon is central to life in India generally. It has also inspired ragas in Carnatic and Hindustani classical music, such as Meghamalhar and amruthavarshini.
s: One non-crop item: rivers fill / life thrives
A second: ragas inspired by the monsoon

questions.q: Suppose that in summer the Asian landmass stayed as cool as the ocean instead of heating up. Using the chapter's ideas of temperature, pressure and wind, say what would happen to (i) the pressure over the land, (ii) the winds, and (iii) the rain in India. Why does this show the importance of the land heating faster?
questions.a: If the land did not heat up, no powerful low-pressure system would form over it. Air flows from high pressure to low pressure, so winds would not be drawn from the ocean towards the land. Without these moist ocean winds, the moisture would not condense over the land and fall as heavy monsoon rain, so the usual summer rain would be weak or missing. This shows that the monsoon rests on land heating up faster than the ocean.
s: No low pressure forms over the land
Air flows high to low, so no strong ocean-to-land winds
No moisture-laden winds, so no heavy monsoon rain
Concludes that the monsoon depends on the land heating faster than the ocean

questions.q: Which sequence matches the chapter's account of the Uttarakhand disaster of 2013?
questions.a: In 2013 continuous heavy rain over several days caused a sudden glacial burst; many landslides followed, Kedarnath's surroundings were destroyed and about 6,000 people lost their lives.
o: Several days of continuous heavy rain, a glacial burst, many landslides, and the areas around Kedarnath destroyed
Several dry days, a forest fire, many landslides, and the areas around Kedarnath cleared of people before the rains
A cyclone landing on the coast, floods in the cities, a glacial burst, and the roads and bridges of the plains washed away
Landslides first, then continuous heavy rain, then a drought, and the areas around Kedarnath saved by early warning

questions.q: A hill council plans to clear forest on a slope for a new road and to put up many buildings along it, before the monsoon. Give two concerns, taken from the chapter, that the council should record.
questions.a: Cutting down forests and constructing too many buildings that block the natural flow of water are human activities that increase the chances of landslides, which are common in hilly regions and often occur during the monsoon, so a monsoon-time clearance is especially risky. Building infrastructure without following approved methods adds to the risk.
s: Concern 1: cutting forests / too many buildings raise landslide chances
Concern 2: landslides often occur in the monsoon, or infrastructure must follow approved methods

questions.q:
The India Meteorological Department tells a coastal village of 1,350 residents that a cyclone will cross the coast within 36 hours, 120 km to the north. The school (400 people) and the panchayat hall (500) are the only safe buildings. Fifteen buses of 90 seats each could take everyone inland, but the road may flood after the first 10 buses have left. A battalion of the NDRF can reach the village only if called early. (Figures are invented.)
(a) Name any two things the IMD tells about a coming cyclone, and say which one decides whether the village should evacuate.
(b) How many residents are not covered by the two buildings?
(c) If the road floods after 10 buses leave, how many people are left behind?
(d) The sarpanch must choose: bus everyone inland now, or keep 900 people in the two buildings, shelter the other 450 with relatives on higher ground in the village and put the NDRF on standby. What do you advise and why?
questions.a: (a) Any two of formation, evolution and place of landing; the place of landing decides whether the village lies in its path. (b) 1,350 - (400 + 500) = 450. (c) 10 x 90 = 900 leave, so 1,350 - 900 = 450 are left behind. (d) Either with reasons: busing everyone gets all 1,350 out if the road holds, but if it floods the 450 left behind have no shelter at all; the shelter-and-standby plan keeps 900 under a roof for certain and puts the other 450 on higher ground with relatives, with the NDRF (trained for rescue and evacuation in cyclones and floods) ready to help, but it keeps everyone in the village in the cyclone's region. A strong answer says when to call the NDRF early and compares the two 450s.
s: Part (a): two IMD facts; place of landing decides
Part (b): 450
Part (c): 450 left behind
Part (d): a reasoned choice comparing the two 450s and the NDRF

questions.q: After heavy rain a city street is under knee-deep water, yet the nearby river is well within its banks. The chapter's most likely cause is that the ___ system is overburdened.
questions.a: drainage

questions.q: True or False: 'In a Himalayan region a flood can occur even when no river has burst its banks.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Glacial lakes form a barrier of rocks and ice to hold their water; if the glaciers melt too fast or there is too much rainfall, the pressure can break the barrier (a glacial burst), flooding the valley below without a river overflowing.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a glacial lake breaks through its barrier of rocks and ice (glacial burst)

questions.q: Aarav says, 'The calmest, cloudless part of a cyclone is its outer rim, where the winds are slowest.' Which correction agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says winds collect moisture, form clouds and rotate inwards towards the centre of the depression; this centre, which is cloudless, is the eye of the cyclone.
o: The cloudless part is the centre, called the eye, and the winds rotate inwards towards it.
The cloudless part is the rim, and the clouds form at the centre as the winds rotate outwards from it.
There is no cloudless part; clouds and rain extend right to the centre of every cyclone without a break.
The cloudless part is the place of landing, which is often about 120 km away from the centre.

questions.q: A fire in a forest of Uttarakhand starts when someone drops a lit cigarette in a drought year with strong winds. Which conclusion agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says forest fires are often fuelled by dry climatic conditions, droughts or high winds, and that human carelessness is another frequent cause.
o: Dry conditions, droughts, high winds and human carelessness can all be causes.
The fire is purely natural, since droughts and high winds are the only causes of forest fires.
The fire is purely human, since human carelessness is the only frequent cause of forest fires.
The fire is neither, since forest fires break out only in states without large forested areas.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Cyclones strike only the eastern coast of India.
2. The NDRF is the body that forecasts cyclones and tracks their formation.
3. The India Meteorological Department keeps track of coming cyclones and tells us their place of landing.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: the eastern coast sees several cyclones every year, but the statement says only. 2 is false: the NDRF is a force trained to respond to disasters; the IMD tracks cyclones. 3 is correct.
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Villages A and B on the same Himalayan range receive the same days of heavy monsoon rain. Village A keeps its slope forest. Village B has cleared its slope for many new buildings that block the natural flow of water. Which statement agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Landslides are often triggered by heavy rain, earthquakes or volcanic activity, and in hill regions the chances have increased because of cutting down forests and too many buildings that block the natural flow of water.
o: B is likelier to see a landslide, since cutting forests and too many buildings raise the chances.
A is likelier to see a landslide, since forests add weight to a slope, and the rain is only the trigger in both villages.
Both are equally likely to see a landslide, since heavy rain is the only cause and human activity does not matter.
Neither can see a landslide, since landslides are caused only by earthquakes and volcanic activity.

questions.q:
Match each disaster in Column A with a human-related cause the chapter links to it in Column B.
Column A: 1. A landslide on a hill slope  2. Flooding of a city street  3. A forest fire  4. A glacial burst
Column B: a. glaciers melting too fast (as is increasingly the case)  b. human carelessness  c. cutting down forests and building too many structures on slopes  d. concrete or asphalt surfaces that do not let water soak in
questions.a: 1-c (cutting forests, too many buildings), 2-d (surfaces that do not absorb water), 3-b (human carelessness), 4-a (glaciers melting too fast).

questions.q: Rahul states two sentences. (i) 'Forest fires in states such as Uttarakhand and Madhya Pradesh are fuelled by dry conditions, droughts and high winds.' (ii) 'So forest fires are purely natural.' Judge each sentence separately using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. (i) is correct: dry climatic conditions, droughts and high winds fuel forest fires. (ii) is wrong: the chapter says human carelessness is another frequent cause, so fires are not purely natural.
s: Verdict: partly right, each sentence judged separately
(i) correct: dry conditions, droughts, high winds fuel fires
(ii) wrong: human carelessness is another frequent cause

questions.q:
In a drought-hit village the monsoon has failed. Women now walk 4 km to the well and 4 km back, twice a day. Thirty agricultural labourers have left for the city. Rice that cost Rs 50 per kg now costs Rs 59 (all figures invented).
(i) How far does each woman walk in a day?
(ii) By what percentage has the price of rice risen?
(iii) Link each of the three observations to the consequence of monsoon failure named in the chapter.
(iv) Why might a factory 200 km away also be affected?
questions.a: (i) 4 x 2 x 2 = 16 km. (ii) (59 - 50) / 50 = 18 percent. (iii) Women having to walk long distances in search of water; agricultural labourers migrating to the cities; food becoming costlier, fuelling inflation. (iv) Industrial activity depends on predictable weather and the availability of water.
s: Part (i): 16 km
Part (ii): 18 percent
Part (iii): the three observations linked to the chapter's consequences
Part (iv): industry depends on weather and water

questions.q: A student writes, 'The 2013 Uttarakhand disaster was just a landslide.' (a) Correct this using the chapter's account of the event. (b) Name two kinds of infrastructure that the chapter says were swept away.
questions.a: (a) It began with a sudden glacial burst caused by continuous heavy rain over several days, and many landslides followed; the areas around the Kedarnath temple were completely destroyed and about 6,000 people lost their lives. (b) Roads and bridges.
s: Part (a): glacial burst after continuous heavy rain, then landslides
Part (b): roads and bridges

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A monsoon failure can make food grains, vegetables and fruits costlier.
Reason (R): Industrial activity often depends on predictable weather and the availability of water.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The Reason is a separate fact about industry; costlier food follows from failing agriculture, so R does not explain A.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A news report on a forest fire in Chhattisgarh says: 'Smoke hung over nearby towns for days and several tribal hamlets had to be abandoned.' (a) Which two consequences listed in the chapter does the report mention? (b) Name one consequence it does not mention.
questions.a: (a) Spoiling the air quality and displacing local communities. (b) Any one of: destruction of large areas of forest, harm to wildlife, degradation of the ecosystem.
s: Part (a): spoilt air quality and displaced communities
Part (b): one unmentioned consequence (forest destroyed, wildlife harmed or ecosystem degraded)

questions.q: A student says, 'Floods happen only when it rains heavily.' Using the chapter, give three situations in which a flood can arise, showing that heavy rain is not always the whole story.
questions.a: Heavy rain gives run-off the land cannot absorb, but floods also occur when water accumulates in rivers and lakes until banks are breached; in the Himalayas when glaciers melt too fast and a glacial lake breaks its barrier of rocks and ice; and in cities when drains are overburdened, construction blocks waterways or concrete and asphalt do not let water soak in.
s: Run-off or rivers and lakes overflowing
Glacial lake overflow/burst when glaciers melt too fast
City causes: overburdened drains, blocked waterways, non-absorbing surfaces

questions.q: A student says, 'Festivals are cultural, so climate has nothing to do with them.' (a) What link between festivals and climate does the chapter state? (b) Why might a monsoon failure dampen a harvest festival?
questions.a: (a) India has many festivals associated with seasons and agricultural activities, so climate is visible in local cultures. (b) A monsoon failure means poor rainfall, agriculture suffers and food becomes costlier, so there is less harvest to celebrate.
s: Part (a): festivals are associated with seasons and agricultural activities
Part (b): monsoon failure hurts agriculture, so a poor harvest

questions.q:
A Himalayan valley village has 2,000 residents, and 500 pilgrims stay there in the pilgrimage season. A district officer has Rs 3 crore, enough for only one project. Project 1: an early-warning system for the glacial lake above the village, with shelters on high ground for 800 people. Project 2: an all-weather road, the only way out of the valley, which today closes in heavy rain; the road would let all those present leave in a few hours, but part of the hillside forest would have to be cleared. (Figures are invented.)
(a) What percentage of the people present in the season are pilgrims?
(b) What percentage of the people present can the shelters hold?
(c) Which human activity in Project 2 does the chapter link to landslides, and what does the chapter's example of 2013 say about roads in such a valley?
(d) Which project would you fund? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) 500 / 2500 = 20 percent. (b) 800 / 2500 = 32 percent. (c) Cutting down forests; in 2013 many roads and bridges were washed away by the glacial burst and landslides, so a road can itself be lost. (d) Either with reasons: Project 1 gives warning and high-ground shelter, but covers only 32 percent of those present; Project 2 could move everyone out but clears forest that raises landslide chances and may be washed away as in 2013. Credit a decision that uses the 32 percent and the 2013 evidence.
s: Part (a): 20 percent
Part (b): 32 percent
Part (c): forest cutting raises landslide chances; roads and bridges washed away in 2013
Part (d): a decision using the shelter coverage and the risks

questions.q: Write the headline and two opening lines of a news report on a monsoon failure that mentions three consequences the chapter links to it. Then say which consequence reaches people in cities who have no farms.
questions.a: Any valid report mentioning three of: agriculture suffers; women generally have to walk long distances for water; agricultural labourers migrate to the cities; food (grains, vegetables, fruits) becomes costlier, fuelling inflation; industrial activity is hit. The consequence reaching city people is costlier food, which fuels inflation (and migrants arriving).
s: A headline and opening lines that read as a news report
Three consequences correctly taken from the chapter
Costlier food / inflation named as the one reaching city people

questions.q:
Three reports arrive in one week. Report 1: a lake above a mountain village broke through its wall of rocks and ice. Report 2: rivers in Assam rose after days of rain and overflowed their banks. Report 3: a city street flooded where nullahs had been built over and the roads are all concrete.
(i) Name the kind of flood and its cause in each report.
(ii) Which of the three does the chapter say is increasingly likely because of a process it names, and what is that process?
(iii) Which is mainly the result of human decisions, and why?
questions.a: (i) Report 1: a glacial burst, when pressure from glacier water breaks the barrier. Report 2: a river flood, from heavy rainfall and overflowing rivers or lakes (Assam is named among vulnerable states). Report 3: a city flood, from poorly planned construction blocking waterways and surfaces of concrete or asphalt that do not let water soak in. (ii) The glacial burst, because glaciers are increasingly melting too fast. (iii) The city flood, because construction on waterways and the choice of concrete surfaces and drainage are human decisions.
s: Report 1: glacial burst with its cause
Report 2: river flood from heavy rainfall and overflowing rivers
Report 3: city flood with its two causes
Part (ii): glacial burst; glaciers melting too fast
Part (iii): city flood, human decisions on construction and surfaces

questions.q: A student says, 'Firewood is a fossil fuel because it comes from plants.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter defines fossil fuels as sources of energy formed from the remains of plants and animals that died millions of years ago and were buried deep, where heat and pressure turned them into coal, petroleum oil and natural gas.
o: Fossil fuels formed from plants and animals that died millions of years ago and lay buried; firewood does not.
Fossil fuels are any fuels made from plants and animals, so firewood counts, though it releases fewer greenhouse gases.
Fossil fuels are fuels burnt in industry and transportation, so firewood counts only when a factory uses it.
Fossil fuels formed from gases in the natural carbon cycle, so firewood cannot count because it has no carbon.

questions.q:
A woollen workshop in a north Indian town earns a profit of Rs 200 on each sweater it sells. In the winters before 2025 it sold 800, 790 and 800 sweaters. In early 2025, when India's average temperature was 1 to 3 degrees C above normal and the winter was much shorter and milder, it sold only 560. For next winter the owner can (A) place the usual wool order, or (B) spend Rs 1.5 lakh on machines to make light cotton wear as well; she expects the cotton line to add Rs 36,000 of profit in each mild winter. (All figures are invented.)
(a) By what percentage did sales fall in 2025 compared with a normal winter of 800?
(b) How much profit did the workshop lose in 2025 compared with a normal winter, and which kinds of activity does the chapter say such warming affects?
(c) After how many mild winters would the cotton machines repay their cost?
(d) Which option would you choose? Justify with your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) (800 - 560) / 800 = 30 percent. (b) 240 x 200 = Rs 48,000; the chapter says agricultural production and many small-scale industries are affected. (c) 150,000 / 36,000 = about 4.2, so the machines repay their cost only after five mild winters. (d) Either with reasons: A depends on winters returning to normal; one mild winter is a single example and the cotton line needs five mild winters to pay back, but the chapter says rising temperatures are perceptible and the planet is warming over the long term, so more mild winters are likely, and the cotton line adds resilience. A mix (some cotton, less wool) is also defensible if the numbers are used.
s: Part (a): 30 percent
Part (b): Rs 48,000; agriculture and small-scale industries
Part (c): about 4.2, so five mild winters
Part (d): a choice weighing payback against long-term warming

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. A change in climate can be on the scale of the whole planet or only of a region.
2. The natural greenhouse effect is needed for life, while the extra heat trapped since the 19th century comes from enormous releases by human activities.
3. Mitigation aims to reduce the causes of climate change, while resilience is the capacity to recover quickly from difficulties.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: All three are correct: climate change may be planetary or regional; the natural effect warms Earth enough for life while human releases add extra heat; mitigation slows warming and cuts its causes, resilience is the capacity to withstand or recover.

questions.q: A geologist finds evidence that Earth's climate changed greatly five million years ago. Which cause does the chapter give for climate change of that kind of period?
questions.a: The chapter says that in past millennia, going back millions of years, natural processes drove climate change; human activities largely drive it only since the 19th century.
o: Natural processes
The burning of fossil fuels
Deforestation by human settlements
Wasteful patterns of consumption

questions.q: A pupil argues, 'The greenhouse effect is the problem, so the best plan is to remove every greenhouse gas from the air.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: In the natural carbon cycle, carbon dioxide and other gases are released gradually and trap heat, warming Earth enough to support life. Humans have released enormous amounts in a few centuries, trapping extra heat.
o: The natural greenhouse effect warms Earth enough to support life; the trouble is the enormous extra release in a few centuries.
The greenhouse effect did not exist before industry, so removing the gases would simply return Earth to its natural state.
The natural greenhouse effect cools Earth enough to support life; the trouble is that humans release too few gases.
The greenhouse effect only began with the burning of coal, so removing the gases would end the effect and warming together.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's winter in early 2025 was much shorter and milder than usual.
Reason (R): The country's average temperature was 1 to 3 degrees C above normal.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the rise in average temperature is the chapter's own explanation of the shorter, milder winter.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Anil says, 'India's winter in early 2025 was much shorter and milder than usual, so that one winter proves climate change.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter defines climate change as significant, long-term changes, and presents early 2025 (1 to 3 degrees C above normal, a shorter and milder winter) as only one example of perceptible rising temperatures.
o: It is one example of rising temperatures; climate change itself means significant long-term shifts.
It proves climate change by itself, because the chapter defines climate change as one unusually mild winter.
It has no link with climate change, because the chapter says warmer winters come from natural processes only.
It is an example only of weather, because the chapter says rising temperatures are not perceptible in India.

questions.q: A district puts solar panels on all its government schools and also builds raised cyclone shelters for coastal villages. Using the chapter's terms, which describes these two actions?
questions.a: Boosting renewable energy cuts the causes of climate change (mitigation). Shelters help communities withstand and recover from disasters (resilience).
o: Solar panels are mitigation; raised shelters build resilience.
Solar panels build resilience; raised shelters are mitigation.
Both are mitigation, since both reduce greenhouse gases.
Both build resilience, since both help people recover quickly.

questions.q: Anwar's school replaces old bulbs and fans with ones that do the same job on less electricity, and her class plants 200 saplings in the playground. Which two of the chapter's mitigation measures do these match?
questions.a: Using less electricity for the same work is improving energy efficiency; planting saplings is planting trees. No renewable source is installed, and nothing here changes lifestyles.
o: Improving energy efficiency and planting trees
Boosting renewable energy and planting trees
Boosting renewable energy and promoting sustainable lifestyles
Improving energy efficiency and promoting sustainable lifestyles

questions.q: A student says, 'Earth was much warmer millions of years ago, so today's warming must also be natural.' Evaluate this using the chapter.
questions.a: The reasoning does not hold. The chapter agrees that in past millennia, even millions of years ago, natural processes drove climate change, but says that since the 19th century climate change has been largely driven by human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation. The cause of earlier change does not show the cause of today's.
s: Verdict: reasoning not valid, earlier change was natural
Since the 19th century change is largely human-driven (examples)

questions.q: The chapter says India's average temperature early in 2025 was 1 to 3 degrees C above normal. A hill town's normal February daytime temperature is 12 degrees C. (a) What range of values would match the country's pattern? (b) The town's thermometer shows 17 degrees C on one February day. Why is this not a contradiction of the chapter's figure?
questions.a: (a) 12 + 1 = 13 to 12 + 3 = 15 degrees C. (b) The 1 to 3 degrees figure is the country's average temperature over the period, not a single town's reading on a single day; one day's 17 degrees C (5 above normal) is weather and can lie outside an average.
s: Part (a): 13 to 15 degrees C
Part (b): an average for the country versus one day in one town

questions.q: A family stops wasting food and electricity, walks to nearby shops and repairs things instead of replacing them. (a) Which cause of climate change named in the chapter is this family reducing? (b) Which of the government's climate mitigation measures does this behaviour match?
questions.a: (a) Production and patterns of excessive or wasteful consumption. (b) Promoting sustainable lifestyles.
s: Part (a): excessive or wasteful consumption
Part (b): promoting sustainable lifestyles

questions.q: Sana makes two statements. (i) 'The greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life.' (ii) 'Humans have had no part in the greenhouse effect.' Judge each statement separately using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. (i) is correct: the natural greenhouse effect warms Earth enough to support life. (ii) is wrong: human activities like industry, transportation and agriculture have released enormous amounts of greenhouse gases in a few centuries, trapping extra heat and causing rapid global warming.
s: Verdict: partly right, each statement judged separately
(i) correct: the natural effect warms Earth enough for life
(ii) wrong: human releases add extra heat

questions.q: True or False: 'The greenhouse effect is itself a human invention; without humans Earth would have no greenhouse effect.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The greenhouse effect occurs naturally in the Earth's carbon cycle: gases released gradually trap heat from the Sun and warm Earth enough to support life. Humans have added enormous amounts of gases, which traps extra heat.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a natural effect that supports life; humans added extra gases

questions.q: Suppose human activities had released greenhouse gases only gradually, at the pace of the natural carbon cycle, and never in enormous amounts. Using the chapter, say what would be true of (i) the greenhouse effect and life on Earth, (ii) the heat trapped, and (iii) the climate patterns that plants, animals and societies depend on. Then explain what this shows about the speed of release.
questions.a: (i) The natural greenhouse effect would still warm Earth enough to support life. (ii) There would be no sudden increase trapping extra heat, so no rapid global warming. (iii) The climate patterns to which plants, animals and human societies have adapted over thousands of years would not be disrupted. The chapter blames the sudden release of enormous amounts in just a few centuries, so the speed of release matters as much as the gases themselves.
s: Natural effect still supports life
No extra heat trapped, no rapid warming
Adapted climate patterns not disrupted
Speed of release (few centuries versus gradual) is the issue

questions.q: (a) Why does the chapter say the sudden increase in greenhouse gases 'disrupts' the climate patterns of plants, animals and human societies? (b) Name one activity in India affected by the rise in temperature in early 2025.
questions.a: (a) Plants, animals and human societies have adapted to the existing climate patterns over thousands of years, and the sudden increase traps extra heat and causes rapid global warming, so the patterns they depend on change faster than they can adapt. (b) Agricultural production, or many small-scale industries.
s: Part (a): adapted over thousands of years; rapid warming changes the pattern
Part (b): agriculture or small-scale industries

questions.q: Write three lines for a school assembly speech on climate change: one line naming a cause the chapter gives, one line giving an effect already seen in India, and one line giving a response. Then say which of your lines concerns mitigation.
questions.a: Any valid lines, e.g. 'Burning coal, petroleum and gas has released enormous amounts of greenhouse gases in a few centuries. Early in 2025 India's temperature was 1 to 3 degrees C above normal and the winter was much shorter and milder. We can plant trees and improve energy efficiency.' The response line (planting trees, efficiency, renewable energy, cutting emissions) is the mitigation line.
s: A cause taken from the chapter
An effect in India taken from the chapter
A response, with the mitigation line identified

questions.q: Explain why climate mitigation sometimes clashes with the desire for economic growth. Give two measures from the chapter that governments promote.
questions.a: Governments try to cut greenhouse gas emissions, boost renewable energy, plant trees and improve energy efficiency. But these can conflict with the wish for economic growth and increased consumption, which often involve more industry, transport and use of energy.
s: Two mitigation measures named
Economic growth and consumption are desired
States the clash between them

questions.q:
A school in Pune used 12,000 units of electricity a month. After replacing old fans and lights with ones that do the same work on 20 percent less electricity, it fitted rooftop solar panels that supply 3,000 units a month. The trust has Rs 6 lakh left and two plans. Plan P: more panels that supply a further 1,000 units a month for certain. Plan Q: tree planting and an awareness drive; the trust hopes that 400 students' families will each save 5 units a month, but expects only 60 percent of them to do so, and their savings will not reduce this school's bill. (All figures are invented.)
(a) How many units a month does the school now draw from the grid, and what percentage cut is that on the original 12,000?
(b) To which of the chapter's mitigation measures does each step taken so far, and each plan, belong?
(c) How many units a month would Plan Q save at the expected 60 percent, and how does that compare with Plan P?
(d) Which plan would you recommend? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) 12,000 x 0.8 = 9,600; 9,600 - 3,000 = 6,600 units; (12,000 - 6,600) / 12,000 = 45 percent. (b) Efficient fans and lights: improving energy efficiency; rooftop panels and Plan P: boosting renewable energy; Plan Q: planting trees and promoting sustainable lifestyles. (c) 400 x 5 x 0.6 = 1,200 units a month, 200 more than Plan P's 1,000, but spread over families and not certain. (d) Either with reasons: Plan P is a certain cut of 1,000 units that also brings the school's cut to about 53 percent; Plan Q saves more units on paper and builds habits and green cover, but depends on families acting and does not cut this school's own bill. Credit a choice that uses the 1,200 and 1,000 and the uncertainty.
s: Part (a): 6,600 units and 45 percent
Part (b): efficiency, renewable energy, trees and sustainable lifestyles
Part (c): 1,200 units, 200 more than Plan P
Part (d): a recommendation weighing certainty against reach

questions.q:
The chapter says India's average temperature early in 2025 was 1 to 3 degrees C above normal. A group lists four towns (normal, recorded February average in degrees C; the figures are invented): Town A 18 and 20; Town B 24 and 25; Town C 12 and 17; Town D 30 and 31.
(i) Find each town's departure from normal.
(ii) Which towns fall within the country's 1 to 3 degrees pattern?
(iii) A student says Town C's 5 degrees disproves the chapter. Evaluate.
(iv) Name two kinds of economic activity the chapter says such warmth affects.
questions.a: (i) A +2, B +1, C +5, D +1. (ii) A, B and D. (iii) The 1 to 3 degrees figure is the country's average temperature, so individual towns can lie above or below it; Town C's departure shows warming but does not disprove an average. (iv) Agricultural production and many small-scale industries.
s: Part (ii): A, B and D
Part (iii): national average versus one town
Part (iv): agriculture and small-scale industries
